div.head: Chapter 23
div.p: These eight principles and foundations having been established — which is the first of the two things we promised at the outset of this little treatise — let us now take up the second; namely, to draw certain responsive conclusions for the resolution of each doubt. As to the first doubt, then, let this be the First Conclusion.

First Conclusion, to the first doubt. Francisco Pizarro and all the Spaniards who were with him — who were a hundred and seventy men, more or less — in the seizure of that great King Atahualpa of Peru, and who killed him and burned him along with the others, committed most grave mortal sins, and are bound to make restitution in solidum, each one for the whole. And without it they will not be saved: for the deprivation of the great state and principality of the said king from his heirs, or from whoever had the right to it by law or according to his custom; and for all the great and never before seen or heard-of treasures that they unjustly took from him as his ransom; and for the many others they robbed and usurped from him; and for the others, almost infinite in number, that the Spaniards who came after have robbed of gold and silver and precious stones and livestock and riches; and for all the incredible and irreparable harms and deaths and losses and despoilings of lordships, and the total destruction of those kingdoms that has followed; and they were faithless men, breaking the faith and promise or compact they made with the said King Atahualpa to set him at liberty if he gave them a room full of gold and silver, as men without faith and without fear of God and without truth.

The first part of this conclusion — that they committed most grave mortal sins — is proved by many reasons. The first, because they were proper and perfect cruel tyrants, as was proved in the first principle, § 1, and in § 4, on the fourth category of unbelievers.

A tyrant is one who usurps by force, without just cause, the states and principalities that belong to the true kings and lords by natural law and the law of nations. For where in the world was the name and office of tyrant ever so clearly verified as by us in those parts? Let our own tyrants say so, and I trust they will not deny it. And thus we will add that not only do they usurp foreign lordships and principalities, but most cruelly, without guilt or cause on the part of those they harm, they kill and tear apart, and commonly burn alive with diverse torments, and wipe from the face of the earth natural kings and lords, as we have done throughout all the Indies; and so did Pizarro and his gang to King Atahualpa and to many others. Certainly the name and office of tyrants properly belongs and belonged to them. We have been successors of Nimrod: the first tyrant after the flood, that slayer and oppressor of men. And by this means he made himself king, compelling men to obey and serve him: "He was a mighty hunter before the Lord," Genesis 10, that is, a slayer and destroyer, according to the Gloss; who, according to Josephus, "with new greed for power exercised tyranny, compelling men to submit to him; and the beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, etc." Genesis 10.
For tyrants sin most mortally. Therefore Pizarro and his companions committed most grave mortal sins.

The second is proved by the seventh principle, § 12, where it was concluded by many reasons that the first entry of the Spaniards was tyrannical and abominable, and against the natural order they were bound to observe in their entry. To break the natural order is mortal sin, because it goes against the divine disposition that with his wisdom God placed in all things.

The third is proved — that they sinned mortally — because they acted against the dictate of reason and natural law, which teaches man how he must conduct himself in his practical deeds, toward God and toward men, as it is a light that illuminates the conscience and makes it know the first principles or precepts and their immediate conclusions of things moral and practicable, such as: "The good is to be pursued; and thus God is to be obeyed, parents are to be honored, good is to be done to all; and evil is to be shunned and avoided; and thus against God nothing is to be said or done that is unfitting to him; and no wrong is to be done to anyone, not to kill, not to steal, etc." And these principles or precepts and their immediate conclusions: the natural reason of any man judges that they are to be followed or not followed. And this is the law or natural right that orders men how they ought to conduct themselves fittingly, toward God and toward their neighbors.

Now those who did so much harm and evil to King Atahualpa — seizing him, despoiling him of his states, his lands and lordships, killing him and burning him, despoiling and depriving his heirs of those same states and lordships and of all his other goods, without guilt or cause or reason — acted against the precepts of the law and of natural right, and in the gravest and most essential matters. Therefore they offended most gravely in mortal sins.

The fourth: they acted against the express negative texts of divine law. It is forbidden by divine law that we covet the things of others, and far more so to take them — whether secretly as in stealing, or by force against their will, which is violence and rapine —, as appears from Exodus 20: "You shall not steal. You shall not covet your neighbor's house, nor his field, nor his servant, nor his handmaid, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is his." Et Deuteronomy 5. Likewise: "You shall not remove or shift the landmarks of your neighbor which those who came before set in their possessions." Deuteronomy 19 et Proverbs 22, likewise chapter 23: "Do not touch the landmarks of the little ones, nor enter the field of orphans; for their kinsman — that is, God — is the lord of their lot, and he will judge their cause against you." Thus far there. And Saint Jerome, Ad Rusticum episcopum, found in c. diaconi, 93 Dist.: "Each person is commanded to possess something in this visible world: in such a way that he be content with his possession alone and not invade the things of others, not take the field of the poor, nor the vineyard, nor any other good, nor the servants, nor the fruits." Thus far he.

For those persons not only coveted any foreign things — not only houses, sheep, not servants and farms or estates or the lands where they sowed their crops —: but the states, the dignities, the honors and lordships, the royal principalities, the jurisdictions and all the vassals, the lands and kingdoms with their ancient landmarks preserved, the treasures and everything they had and ruled in the world, and together with all of this, their very lives; and all of this with great violence and injurious hand. Therefore they sinned most gravely and most mortally.

And if for taking away a little heifer and a small ox from a neighbor God makes himself that neighbor's kinsman to avenge him, how much more will he be and will he avenge what was done to harm such persons, and so many of them, in such diverse and precious things, by those men!

Let the fifth reason be, briefly, as follows. All those who act against justice in any notable matter commit mortal sin. For whoever does anything unjust acts against the divine precept and the law of God, which reduces to theft, or rapine, or adultery, or homicide, etc. And any of these transgressions is mortal sin. Likewise, every injustice always consists in some harm done to another; and any harm done to another goes against the charity that moves — or ought to move — us to love him. Therefore to do injustice is mortal sin. Likewise, according to the jurists, the precepts of justice are three: the first, to live honestly and virtuously; the second, to do harm or injury to no one; the third, to render to each person what is theirs.

Now those who inflicted such extraordinary and irreparable evils and harms upon King Atahualpa and all his people, and upon the other kings and lords and peoples, while they were in their own lands and kingdoms without having offended us and without owing us anything: and thus without any true or even colorable just cause, committed not one but many notable and extraordinary injustices repugnant to charity; and so not only did they not live honestly and virtuously, but they did so much harm to that great king and to so many, and took and usurped so many of their most precious goods. Therefore they committed most grave mortal sins.

And that these sins are most grave as regards their neighbors is plain in itself. But as regards God, see what was written in the seventh principle, chapter 15, about the scandals and infamies to the faith that by their evil lives they have caused among those peoples: who believe that the Christian religion is nothing other than robbing and killing and committing all the abominations and ugliness they have committed and commit; and it is certain that they have so defamed the name of Jesus Christ that it is considered the greatest miracle God performs in those Indies that those peoples believe the things of the faith, seeing the deeds of those who bear the name of Christians.

And because the gravity of sins is measured according as they result in dishonor to the honor of God — and these are most grave —, and after these the gravest are those measured by the greatness and gravity of the harm that comes to one's neighbors: and those one hundred and seventy have been the cause that the name of Christ is blasphemed and impeded, that those peoples do not know him or receive or venerate and honor him as the true God; and the harms done to King Atahualpa and to the others were the greatest temporal harms that can be done to anyone in the world; and the Spaniards have been the cause that infinite souls perish without faith and without sacraments forever in the eternal fires: it follows that the sins those men committed were above all sins most grave. On this gravity of sins, see Saint Thomas: 1a 2ae q. 73 a. 8 ad 3m; and in the questions De malo: q. 2 a. 10 corp.; and in the 2.2 q. 34 a. 3 et q. 78 a. 3 et q. 74 a. 2 corp. et q. 154 a. 12.
